candidate_concepts.label: Bandwidth problem definition
candidate_concepts.description: Given a graph, find a linear ordering of vertices that minimizes the maximum length of an edge (the maximum number of intervening vertices between any two adjacent vertices).
coverage_criteria: Student can state the goal of the bandwidth problem.
Student can compute the bandwidth for a small example ordering.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: From 00:40, the lecturer defines the bandwidth problem as minimizing the number of intervening vertices, and provides an example at 01:35.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The bandwidth problem is a concrete optimization task that can be assessed by asking the student to explain and compute bandwidth for a given graph.

candidate_concepts.label: Derangement generation via backtracking
candidate_concepts.description: A derangement is a permutation where no element is in its original position. To generate all derangements using backtracking, restrict candidates to numbers not yet used and not equal to the current index.
coverage_criteria: Student can define a derangement.
Student can write the construct_candidates function for derangements by excluding the current index and already used numbers.
Student can contrast this with generating all permutations and filtering.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: At 12:00, the lecturer defines derangements and then walks through modifying the permutation backtracking code to generate only derangements by changing construct_candidates (16:57).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a direct application of backtracking with a slight modification, making it a focused checkable exercise.

candidate_concepts.label: Efficiency of generating all permutations vs. pruning
candidate_concepts.description: When the number of solutions is a sizable fraction of the search space (e.g., derangements are ~n!/e of permutations), generating all candidates and filtering may not be much slower, but for most problems pruning early is crucial.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why generating all permutations and filtering derangements is only about three times slower.
Student can argue that for bandwidth, early pruning is essential because few permutations are optimal.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: From 20:15, the lecturer discusses why generating all permutations and checking for derangements is not inefficient because derangements are roughly n!/e, a constant fraction of all permutations.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept contrasts two backtracking strategies and can be assessed by asking the student to estimate relative search sizes.

candidate_concepts.label: Eight-Queens problem definition
candidate_concepts.description: Place 8 queens on an 8x8 chessboard so that no two queens threaten each other (same row, column, or diagonal). The goal is to generate all such configurations.
coverage_criteria: Student can state the constraints of the Eight-Queens problem.
Student can verify whether a given configuration is valid.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: At 25:26, the lecturer presents the Eight-Queens problem and its chess constraints.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a classic constraint satisfaction problem often used to teach backtracking, suitable as a basic checkable definition.

candidate_concepts.label: State space reduction via permutation representation in Eight-Queens
candidate_concepts.description: By noting that each row must have exactly one queen, the search space can be reduced from 64^8 to 8! by representing a solution as a permutation of column indices.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why a solution can be encoded as a permutation of {1..8}.
Student can compare the number of states for bit vector (2^64), list of pairs (64^8), and permutation (8!) representations.
Student can justify that 8! = 40,320 is computationally tractable.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: From 35:43 to 41:52, the lecturer shows how representing the board as a row-wise column index reduces the search space to 8! and contrasts it with larger representations.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a key insight about representation choice that can be checked by having the student perform similar state-space analysis for other problems.

candidate_concepts.label: Candidate constructor for Eight-Queens with threat checking
candidate_concepts.description: In the permutation representation, construct_candidates iterates over columns, and for each column checks if it conflicts with any previously placed queen via column or diagonal attack (|row_diff| = |col_diff|).
coverage_criteria: Student can write pseudocode to check column and diagonal threats.
Student can trace the backtracking on a small example (e.g., 4-Queens).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: At 42:38, the lecturer presents the C code for construct_candidates for Eight-Queens, explaining column and diagonal threat checks.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: The threat-checking logic is a specific, implementable detail that can be directly tested by asking the student to write or explain the condition.

candidate_concepts.label: Symmetry pruning in Eight-Queens
candidate_concepts.description: By exploiting vertical symmetry, we can restrict the first queen to columns 1–4 and generate the mirror solution for each result, cutting the search space roughly in half.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain how to generate all solutions by only exploring half the placements and then reflecting.
Student can argue that no solution is missed.
Student can calculate the approximate reduction in states (20,000).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: From 51:25, the lecturer illustrates using a vertical mirror to reduce the search by half, explaining that any solution with first queen on the right has a mirror on the left.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: Symmetry pruning is a general optimization technique that can be checked by asking the student to apply it to a similar problem.

candidate_concepts.label: Chessboard covering problem and backtracking search
candidate_concepts.description: The problem is to place the 8 non-pawn pieces on a chessboard such that every square is threatened. The search uses an array of 8 piece position indices, and can be pruned by placing pieces in order of decreasing power and checking if the remaining pieces can cover the remaining holes.
coverage_criteria: Student can define the covering problem.
Student can describe the representation and candidate construction.
Student can explain the pruning condition: total_max_coverage(remaining_pieces) < uncovered_squares => backtrack.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: From 59:01 to 1:14:14, the lecturer presents the covering problem, discusses representation, piece power ordering, and pruning by remaining coverage.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a comprehensive example of backtracking with advanced pruning, suitable as a capstone checkable concept.

candidate_concepts.label: Pruning principle in backtracking
candidate_concepts.description: To make backtracking efficient, prune partial solutions that cannot possibly lead to a better or valid complete solution as early as possible, using problem-specific constraints.
coverage_criteria: Student can explain why pruning is essential for backtracking performance.
Student can give examples of pruning (threat checks, symmetry, remaining coverage).

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The entire lecture emphasizes pruning: at 06:47 advice on pruning first, and repeated examples (symmetry, coverage) illustrate the principle.
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This is a high-level principle that ties together the examples and can be assessed by asking the student to design a pruning strategy for a new problem.
